findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The owner_id value is interpolated directly into the SQL string via an f-string. A caller passing an owner_id containing a single quote (e.g. "' OR '1'='1") would alter the query's WHERE clause, potentially exposing or modifying data belonging to other customers. Use a parameterized query with a placeholder instead of string formatting.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a crafted owner_id such as "' OR 1=1 --"; the resulting query returns all orders instead of just the attacker's, leaking data across customer boundaries.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: Use a parameterized query to prevent SQL injection in load_order_rows

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default value for events is a mutable list created once at function definition time. Every call that omits the events argument appends to that same shared list, so events from prior calls accumulate. The returned dict also exposes the internal list. Use None as the default and create a fresh list inside the function.
findings.failure_scenario: The first call returns {"shipment": ["shipment"]}. The second call (with no events argument) returns {"invoice": ["shipment", "invoice"]} because the default list retained the previous event, corrupting per-type event counts.
findings.suggestion: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.title: Replace the mutable default list with a None default

findings.body: The loop starts at index 1, so the first entry (index 0) is never scored or included in the ranked result. This silently drops one entry from every invoice, which will cause under-billing or missing line items.
findings.failure_scenario: An invoice with entries [A, B, C] only scores B and C; entry A is never ranked and is omitted from the output, causing it to be missing from the invoice.
findings.title: Start the loop at index 0 to include the first entry

findings.body: The function accepts a threshold parameter but ignores it, hardcoding 5000 instead. Callers passing a different threshold (e.g. 10000) will still get rows flagged at 5000, producing incorrect review queues. Also, row["total"] will raise KeyError if a row lacks the "total" key; consider using row.get("total", 0) if that is possible given the caller's schema.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, 10000.0) expecting only rows above 10000 to be flagged. The function ignores the threshold and flags every row above 5000 instead, flooding the review queue with false positives.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of hardcoded 5000 in flag_large_backorder_totals

findings.body: The query has no LIMIT clause, so fetchall() materializes every matching row. An owner with a large order history will cause the entire result set to be loaded into memory and returned to the caller.
findings.failure_scenario: When a customer has thousands of orders, fetchall() loads all rows at once, increasing memory usage and query latency proportionally to the table size.
findings.title: Add a LIMIT clause to the order query

findings.body: The `seen` list is queried with `in` on every iteration, making each membership test O(n) and the overall function O(n²). A set provides O(1) average-case lookups and reduces the loop to linear time.
findings.failure_scenario: With thousands of payment rows, the quadratic membership checks dominate runtime, causing noticeable latency spikes during batch processing.
findings.suggestion:
seen: set[str] = set()
    labels: list[str] = []
    for row in rows:
        label = str(row.get("label", ""))
        if label not in seen:
            seen.add(label)
            labels.append(label)
    return labels
findings.title: Use a set for membership tracking

findings.body: The docstring promises constant-time behaviour and states that records arrive in chronological order, yet the implementation sorts the entire list, which is O(n log n). If the chronological-order assumption holds, the last element is already the newest and no sort is needed; the current code is both slower and misleading about its complexity.
findings.title: Return the last record directly instead of sorting when chronological order is guaranteed

findings.body: The seen collection is a list, so the in check is O(n) per row, making the whole function O(n^2). A set provides O(1) membership testing and is the standard tool for deduplication; the current list-based approach is unnecessarily expensive for large input.
findings.title: Use a set for O(1) membership checks instead of a list

findings.anchor: def flag_large_backorder_totals(rows: list[dict[str, object]], threshold: float) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
findings.body: The threshold parameter is accepted but never used; the function hardcodes 5000 in the comparison instead. Callers passing a different threshold will get silently wrong results, and the parameter creates a false impression of configurability.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, 10000.0) expecting only rows above 10000 to be flagged. The function ignores the argument and flags rows above 5000 instead, returning roughly twice as many rows as expected and causing incorrect review queues.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of the hardcoded 5000 literal

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The owner_id value is interpolated directly into the SQL string via an f-string. Any caller passing a value containing SQL metacharacters can alter the query's logic — for example, injecting a condition that returns all rows, unioning additional tables, or mutating data if the cursor permits multiple statements. Parameterized queries prevent this by keeping data separate from the query text.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker or buggy caller supplies owner_id = "' OR '1'='1" as the customer_id filter. The resulting query becomes SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '' OR '1'='1', returning every order row instead of just the intended owner's rows.
findings.suggestion: query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
findings.title: Fix SQL injection by using parameterized query

findings.body: The function signature accepts a threshold parameter, but the body ignores it and hardcodes 5000. Callers passing a different threshold will silently get the wrong filtering behaviour, causing backorders above their intended threshold to be missed or smaller ones to be incorrectly flagged.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=1000.0) expecting all rows with total above 1000 to be flagged. The hardcoded 5000 comparison means rows between 1000 and 5000 are never flagged, silently skipping review-worthy backorders.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of hardcoded 5000

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() has been deprecated since Python 3.12 because it returns a naive datetime in UTC, which is ambiguous and error-prone. The recommended replacement is datetime.now(timezone.utc), which returns an aware datetime. Code using utcnow() will emit deprecation warnings on current Python and may break in a future release.
findings.failure_scenario: On Python 3.12+, every call to stamp_manifest_checkpoint emits a DeprecationWarning. In a future Python release utcnow() may be removed entirely, causing an AttributeError at runtime wherever manifest checkpoints are stamped.
findings.title: Replace deprecated datetime.utcnow() with datetime.now(timezone.utc)

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: A mutable list is used as a default parameter value. In Python, default arguments are evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the events argument shares and mutates the same list object. The first caller's event_type will silently appear in every subsequent caller's result, corrupting event tracking across the process lifetime.
findings.failure_scenario: The first call register_shipment_events('shipped') stores 'shipped' in the shared default list. A later call register_shipment_events('delivered') that expects only 'delivered' instead receives {'delivered': ['shipped', 'delivered']} because the default list was never reset between calls.
findings.suggestion: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.title: Replace the mutable default list with None

findings.body: The loop starts at index 1, so entries[0] is never scored and never appears in the returned list. The function's docstring says it ranks invoice entries, but the first entry is silently dropped from the result. Callers relying on a complete ranked list will be missing the first element.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes three invoice entries with scores [90, 50, 30]. The function returns only the entries with scores 50 and 30, dropping the highest-scoring entry at index 0. Downstream logic that expects all entries ranked will operate on incomplete data.
findings.title: Include the first entry in the ranking loop

findings.anchor: def newest_queue_id(records: list[dict[str, object]]) -> str | None:
findings.body: The docstring claims constant-time behavior and states records arrive in chronological order, yet the implementation sorts all records O(n log n). If records are already in chronological order as documented, taking the last element is O(1). Even without that guarantee, a single pass for the maximum is O(n), still better than sorting.
findings.failure_scenario: With large record sets, the unnecessary sort adds O(n log n) overhead on every call, increasing latency proportionally to input size when O(1) or O(n) would suffice.
findings.title: Avoid sorting to find the newest record

findings.body: The seen collection is a list, so the membership test if label in seen is O(n) per iteration. Combined with the outer loop, the function becomes O(n²). A set provides O(1) average-case membership testing, reducing the overall complexity to O(n).
findings.failure_scenario: With thousands of rows, the quadratic membership checks dominate runtime, causing noticeable slowdown that scales with the square of input size.
findings.suggestion:
def unique_payment_labels(rows: list[dict[str, object]]) -> list[str]:
    """Return payment labels in first-seen order without duplicates."""
    seen: set[str] = set()
    labels: list[str] = []
    for row in rows:
        label = str(row.get("label", ""))
        if label in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(label)
        labels.append(label)
    return labels
findings.title: Use a set for seen labels to avoid quadratic lookups

findings.body: The docstring claims the function returns the newest identifier in constant time and assumes records arrive in chronological order. If that assumption holds, the newest record is simply the last element and no sort is needed. The current implementation sorts the entire list, making it O(n log n) and contradicting the documented contract.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller relies on the documented constant-time behaviour and invokes newest_queue_id inside a hot loop over large record sets. Instead of O(1), each call performs an O(n log n) sort, causing a measurable latency regression under load.
findings.title: Use last record directly instead of sorting
